html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. XML: extensible markup language

  • The anatomy of a system prompt and what belongs in it
  • Templates: stable text plus variable slots
  • Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought and when each helps
  • Guardrail prompts and their limits
  • How to treat prompts as versioned, tested artifacts

2System Prompts

Running case

Lumen Advisory Writes the System Prompt for a Bank's Policy Assistant

  • The assistant answers staff questions from a policy library
  • It must cite sources, say when policy is silent, refuse legal advice, and answer in a fixed JSON shape for the agent desktop

Block Write Example
Role and purpose Who the model is and the job "You answer staff questions about retail-banking policy"
Audience Who reads the output "Contact-center agents, not customers"
Rules and boundaries Must and must-not, with the reason "Never give legal advice: staff cannot rely on it with customers"
Sources How to use the context "Use only the provided policy excerpts; quote the clause"
Uncertainty What to do when unsure "If the excerpts do not cover it, say so and suggest escalation"
Format Structure, length, schema "Return JSON with fields answer, citations, confidence"
  • Be clear and direct: Claude is a brilliant new employee with no context; state the task, the constraints and why.
  • Put long documents first and the question and instructions last; separate content with XML-style tags (<policy>, <question>).
  • A role sentence focuses tone and behavior.
  • Hard requirements belong in code (validation, permissions), with the prompt as the first layer, not the only one (Module 13).

3Templates and Reuse

  • A template holds stable instructions and named variable slots (user input, retrieved passages, customer tier).
  • Stable parts first, variable parts last: this keeps a cacheable prefix (Module 6).
  • Separate data from instructions with tags so injected text is treated as data.
  • Keep prompts in version control, with tests (evals) and a change log; roll back when quality drops.
  • Modular prompts: shared blocks (tone, safety rules) reused across assistants; per-use blocks (task, schema).
Exam tip

Templates put the static content first and the dynamic content last. That ordering is also what makes prompt caching work.

4Prompting Techniques

Technique What it is Use when Watch for
Zero-shot Instructions only, no examples Clear, common tasks; strong models Format drift on unusual outputs
Few-shot 3 to 5 relevant, diverse examples in tags Steering format, tone, edge cases; classification boundaries Examples that are too similar bias the output; keep them in an examples block, not instructions
Chain-of-thought Ask for step-by-step reasoning before the answer Multi-step reasoning, math, analysis, checks Extra tokens and latency; with thinking models prefer effort and adaptive thinking over manual step prompts
Self-check / critique Ask the model to review a draft against criteria Quality pass before output Not a replacement for external validation
Prompt chaining Separate calls for stages Complex tasks needing inspection Latency
  • Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer structure and tone; they must be relevant, diverse and clearly marked.
  • Structured outputs (schema-constrained decoding) enforce shape; they do not guarantee truth (validate values).
  • To reduce hallucination: allow "I don't know", ask for direct quotes before conclusions, require citations, and ground in provided sources.
  • Test prompts on a dataset, not on a few hand-picked examples.

5Guardrails in Prompts

Guardrail Purpose Limits
Scope statement Keep the assistant on topic Users can still try to override
Refusal rules with reasons Stop prohibited help Not enforceable alone
Source-grounding rules Reduce invention Still needs verification
Untrusted-content notice Treat tool and document text as data Pair with isolation and least privilege
Output format and schema Predictable downstream use Shape only
  • Prompt guardrails are the first layer. Enforcement (hooks, validation, authorization, human approval) is in code (Module 13).
Exam tip

Prompts are soft controls: they guide behavior but cannot enforce a hard rule, so pair them with code.

Exam tip

Few-shot examples steer format and tone best; chain-of-thought helps multi-step reasoning at the price of tokens.

6Exam Q&A

S1A prompt template places the user's question first, followed by a 6,000-token policy that is identical on every request. Latency and cost are both concerns. What change helps most?

  • ATruncate the policy to its first few hundred tokens
  • BMove the policy to the end of the prompt, after the user question
  • CPut the static policy and instructions first, the user question last, and cache the stable prefix
  • DPut the policy inside a few-shot example block so it is repeated for emphasis
Show the answer

Answer: C. A stable prefix can be cached only if it comes first and does not change.

S2An assistant must output labeled risk levels in a house style that is hard to describe. Which technique fits best?

  • AChain-of-thought with no examples
  • BZero-shot with a longer description of the style in prose only, repeated at the end of the prompt
  • CIncreasing temperature to vary the style
  • DFew-shot prompting with a few relevant, diverse labeled examples
Show the answer

Answer: D. Examples are the most reliable way to convey format and tone.

S3Why should instructions in a system prompt include the reason for a rule?

  • AReasons let users edit the rule
  • BReasons are required by the API schema
  • CReasons make the prompt longer, which improves caching because longer prompts are always cached longer
  • DThe model can apply the rule sensibly in situations the rule did not mention
Show the answer

Answer: D. Explaining the why lets Claude generalize the intent.

S4A schema-constrained output returns well-formed JSON with a wrong account balance. What does this show?

  • AThe schema was too strict
  • BThe model must be retrained
  • CStructured output guarantees shape, not truth, so values must be validated against the source
  • DFew-shot examples were missing from the schema, so the model could not learn the correct balance values
Show the answer

Answer: C. A schema guarantees the shape of the output but not the truth of its values, so content must be validated against the source.

S5Which TWO reduce hallucination in a document-grounded assistant? Select TWO.

  • ATelling the model it must always provide an answer
  • BRaising temperature so that answers are more creative
  • CRemoving the source documents to shorten the prompt
  • DAllowing the model to answer "the documents do not say" and requiring citations
  • EAsking for direct quotes before the conclusion
Show the answer

Answer: D, E. Permission to abstain and quote-first grounding make unsupported claims visible.

S6When is chain-of-thought prompting most useful?

  • ASimple extraction of one field from a short text where the answer is explicit in the first sentence
  • BLatency-critical single-token classification where the answer must be returned within milliseconds
  • CPrompts that must stay under a few tokens
  • DMulti-step reasoning or analysis where intermediate steps improve the result
Show the answer

Answer: D. Step-by-step reasoning helps complex tasks and costs extra tokens.

S7Which statement about prompt guardrails is correct?

  • AThey replace the need for authorization checks
  • BThey are a first layer; hard requirements still need enforcement in code
  • CThey fully prevent prompt injection when worded strongly enough and placed at the top of the prompt
  • DThey are only useful for tone
Show the answer

Answer: B. Prompts can be overridden; enforce critical rules outside the model.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
System prompt Role · audience · rules with reasons · sources · uncertainty · format
Order Long documents and stable text first; question and variables last
Template Stable text plus variable slots; tags separate data from instructions
Few-shot 3 to 5 relevant, diverse, tagged examples
CoT For multi-step reasoning; costs tokens; use effort and thinking on thinking models
Hallucination Allow abstaining, quote first, cite, ground
Schema Shape not truth: validate values
Prompts as code Version, test with evals, roll back
